analysis.one_liner: Ends several tax breaks for large oil companies and puts the savings toward cutting the federal deficit.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in December 2022 and referred to the Finance Committee, where it died with no hearing, no vote, and no action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would deny a set of special tax breaks to large oil companies — those with more than $50 million in annual receipts. Those companies would lose the option to immediately deduct intangible drilling costs, lose the percentage depletion allowance, and lose credits for enhanced oil recovery. It would also tighten rules that let major oil companies claim foreign tax credits for payments to foreign governments that are not generally imposed income taxes, and repeal royalty relief for deep-water and deep-gas drilling on the Outer Continental Shelf. Every dollar saved would go to reducing the federal deficit or the federal debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers as a group: the revenue the bill raises from large oil companies must be used to shrink the deficit or pay down debt, which modestly lowers the fiscal burden passed to everyone. It would not put money directly into anyone's pocket.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires that all savings be deposited in the Treasury and used for federal deficit or debt reduction [S3].
It narrows foreign tax credit rules so major integrated oil companies cannot claim credits for payments to foreign countries that do not impose a generally applicable income tax [S2].
It repeals the Outer Continental Shelf deep-water and deep-gas royalty relief created by the Energy Policy Act of 2005, so the government collects royalties it was excused from collecting [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies, which would lose immediate write-offs for drilling costs, percentage depletion, credits for enhanced oil recovery and for using captured carbon in oil recovery, favorable foreign tax credit treatment, and Outer Continental Shelf royalty relief. Small producers are carved out: the new limits apply only to taxpayers with gross receipts above $50 million.

drawbacks.text: The new limits apply only to taxpayers with more than $50 million in gross receipts, so small and independent producers keep the same deductions and credits the bill takes away from large companies — a carve-out that blunts the policy and preserves a preference for a slice of the industry [S3].

Raising costs for large oil companies does not guarantee anyone else benefits directly: savings are directed to deficit reduction, a broad and diffuse gain, and in a period of high gas prices the industry could argue such costs feed into consumer prices — a general economic pass-through concern, not something the bill text addresses [S3].

The bill repeals deep-water royalty relief but says Interior 'shall not be required' to provide relief in future lease sales, which is weaker language than an outright prohibition, and the change only reaches lease sales not yet finalized [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy is straightforward: take away tax preferences that let large oil companies pay less, and use the money to reduce borrowing. The main cost falls on a concentrated industry, and the main benefit — a smaller deficit — is real but diffuse; no household sees a direct check from it. The $50 million carve-out for smaller producers is a design weakness, but it also keeps the bill from hitting independent drillers. On balance the public interest and the bill's aim run together, though the payoff is indirect.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the last weeks of the 117th Congress and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and the Congress ended before anything happened to it.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez introduced the bill on December 8, 2022, joined by six Democratic cosponsors — Padilla, Booker, Shaheen, Hirono, Cardin, and Murray [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil companies kept the tax preferences and royalty relief the bill would have taken away, and the Treasury forgoes whatever revenue the bill would have raised for deficit reduction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large oil companies keep their tax breaks

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Close Big Oil Tax Loopholes Act on December 8, 2022.

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Padilla, Booker, Shaheen, Hirono, Cardin, Murray).

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the Congress ended with it still pending.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the 50-seat Republican minority plus the lack of committee action were enough to keep it from moving.

industries.note: They would lose immediate expensing of intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, enhanced oil recovery credits, favorable foreign tax credit treatment, and Outer Continental Shelf royalty relief. Their interest in keeping these preferences runs against the public's, since the forgone revenue would otherwise reduce deficits everyone shares.

industries.industry: Small and independent oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill exempts taxpayers with $50 million or less in gross receipts, so smaller producers keep the drilling deductions and depletion allowance that large companies would lose, giving them a relative tax advantage. Their gain comes partly at the Treasury's expense.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and enhanced oil recovery operators
industries.note: The bill ends the 45Q sequestration credit for using captured carbon oxide as a tertiary injectant in oil recovery for new facilities, a provision that subsidizes carbon capture aimed at producing more oil. Projects capturing CO2 for permanent storage keep the credit.
